_meta.description: Mapping of finding types to Article 21(2) risk-management measures in the EU NIS2 Directive. References are the relevant sub-paragraphs of Article 21(2), which lists the minimum cybersecurity risk-management measures required of essential and important entities.
_meta.mapping_rationale: Article 21(2) is the operative provision for risk-management measures. Each finding maps to one or more of its sub-paragraphs (a) through (j). Where a finding legitimately implicates multiple sub-paragraphs, all are listed. This mapping is defensible but interpretive: NIS2 does not prescribe specific technical controls, and a compliance officer or auditor may reasonably arrive at a different mapping. The mapping is documented here to make the reasoning traceable.

audit_notes.S3_PUBLIC_VIA_ACL: 21(2)(i) is the primary requirement — an AllUsers grant is a direct failure of access control policies. This mapping is unambiguous.
audit_notes.S3_PUBLIC_ACCESS_BLOCK_DISABLED: Two references. 21(2)(e) covers security in ongoing system maintenance — PAB is a configuration choice that lives here. 21(2)(f) covers assessing the effectiveness of measures — PAB is one of the mechanisms by which an organisation ensures its access controls remain effective under future changes.
audit_notes.S3_ENCRYPTION_DISABLED: 21(2)(h) explicitly names cryptography and encryption. This mapping is unambiguous — NIS2 requires organisations to have policies for encryption use, and absent encryption on stored data is a direct policy gap.
audit_notes.S3_VERSIONING_DISABLED: 21(2)(c) is a direct match — the sub-paragraph explicitly names backup management and disaster recovery. S3 versioning is exactly this: an object-level recovery mechanism against accidental or malicious deletion and overwrite. This mapping is unambiguous.
audit_notes.S3_LOGGING_DISABLED: 21(2)(b) covers incident handling. Access logs are the raw material incident handling depends on: without them, there is no way to answer 'what was accessed' during an investigation. This mapping is direct.
audit_notes.S3_LIFECYCLE_MISSING: Weakest mapping in this file. NIS2 has no sub-paragraph naming data retention specifically, so this is mapped to 21(2)(a) — policies on risk analysis and the security of network and information systems — as the general policy catch-all: the gap is the absence of a documented retention policy, not a named technical control. Flagged here rather than forced to look as clean as the other S3 mappings.
audit_notes.S3_TLS_NOT_ENFORCED: 21(2)(h) is reused deliberately, not by oversight — the same sub-paragraph already used for S3_ENCRYPTION_DISABLED. NIS2's cryptography clause does not distinguish encryption at rest from encryption in transit, and TLS enforcement is encryption policy applied to data in motion rather than data at rest.
audit_notes.KMS_KEY_ROTATION_DISABLED: 21(2)(h) again — key rotation is a cryptography and encryption policy matter as directly as any finding in this file. First non-S3 finding mapped, same clause as the two S3 cryptography findings above.
audit_notes.KMS_KEY_PENDING_DELETION: 21(2)(c) reused from S3_VERSIONING_DISABLED. A completed key deletion permanently destroys access to everything it encrypted — the clearest possible business-continuity and disaster-recovery failure this file maps to anything.
audit_notes.IAM_ROOT_ACCESS_KEYS_ACTIVE: 21(2)(i) is a direct match — root access keys are the highest-privilege credential in the account, and their existence is squarely an access-control-policy failure.
audit_notes.IAM_ACCOUNT_MFA_NOT_ENABLED: 21(2)(j) explicitly names multi-factor authentication. First use of this sub-paragraph in the file — no other finding maps to it, since this is the only one that is specifically an MFA gap rather than a broader access-control or cryptography issue.
audit_notes.IAM_PASSWORD_POLICY_WEAK: 21(2)(g) covers basic cyber hygiene practices and training. A minimum password length policy is about as textbook a basic-cyber-hygiene control as exists — first use of this sub-paragraph in the file.
audit_notes.IAM_ACCESS_KEY_AGE_EXCEEDS_90_DAYS: 21(2)(i) reused. An unrotated access key is exactly the kind of credential asset this sub-paragraph's 'asset management' language covers — it's a standing credential that hasn't been through any lifecycle management process.
audit_notes.IAM_CONSOLE_LOGIN_ENABLED: 21(2)(i) reused a third time. A console login profile on what should be a programmatic-only identity is an access-control-policy gap in the same family as root's active keys — an access method that exists without a legitimate asset-management justification.
audit_notes.ACCOUNT_CLOUDTRAIL_DISABLED: 21(2)(b) reused from S3_LOGGING_DISABLED, and a stronger case than that one: CloudTrail is the account-wide audit log incident handling depends on, not just one bucket's access logs. If anything this is the cleanest possible match for this sub-paragraph in the whole file.
audit_notes.ACCOUNT_S3_BLOCK_PUBLIC_ACCESS_DISABLED: Same two references as S3_PUBLIC_ACCESS_BLOCK_DISABLED, reused deliberately rather than independently reasoned: this is the same control at account scope instead of bucket scope, not a different finding that happens to look similar.
